## Overview

In this module we demonstrate how to create and apply window functions.


## Window Functions

* Spark SQL supports the following window functions:
    * `cume_dist`
    * `dense_rank`
    * `lag`
    * `lead`
    * `ntile`
    * `percent_rank`
    * `rank`
    * `row_number`

* Aggregate and window functions are applied `over` a window specification

* A window specification consists of at least one of the following:
    * Partitioning column
    * Ordering column
    * Row specification

# Lesson
---

%md
## Example: Cumulative Count and Sum

paragraphs.title: Create a simple DataFrame
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

df = spark.range(10)
df.show()

paragraphs.title: Create a simple window specification
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Window for comparing the current record (currentRow) with all preceding records (unboundedPreceding)
ws = Window.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
type(ws)

paragraphs.title: Use the window specification to compute cumulative count and sum
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.functions import count, sum

# over(ws) applies the window to calculate cumulative counts and sums.
df.select("id", count("id").over(ws).alias("cum_cnt"), sum("id").over(ws).alias("cum_sum")).show()

paragraphs.title: Tip: Examine the default column name to gain additional insight (if you are SQL literate)
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

df.select("id", count("id").over(ws), sum("id").over(ws)).printSchema()

%md
## Example: Compute average days between rides for each rider

paragraphs.title: Create window specification
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Window by rider_id
ws = Window.partitionBy("rider_id").orderBy("date_time")

paragraphs.title: Use the `lag` function to extract the date and time of the previous ride
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.functions import lag

# 'lag' allows for comparison with the previous record
rides2 = rides.withColumn("date_time_previous", lag("date_time").over(ws))
rides2.select("rider_id", "date_time", "date_time_previous").show(truncate=False)

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
A rider's first ride does not have a previous ride; therefore, the value is set to null.

paragraphs.title: Compute the number of days between consecutive rides
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.functions import datediff
rides3 = rides2.withColumn("days_between_rides", datediff("date_time", "date_time_previous"))
rides3.select("rider_id", "date_time", "date_time_previous", "days_between_rides").show(truncate=False)

paragraphs.title: Compute the average days between rides for each rider
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.functions import count, mean
rides4 = rides3 \
  .groupBy("rider_id") \
  .agg(count("*").alias("num_rides"), mean("days_between_rides").alias("mean_days_between_rides"))

paragraphs.title: Compute top and bottom 10 riders
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

rides4 \
  .where(rides4.mean_days_between_rides.isNotNull()) \
  .orderBy("mean_days_between_rides") \
  .show(10)

rides4 \
  .orderBy("mean_days_between_rides", ascending=False) \
  .show(10)

paragraphs.title: Question
paragraphs.text:
%md How can we make this analysis better? For example: **Filtering or weighting by a minimum number of trips (`num_rides`)** - The results include drivers with very few trips who show high average values—such as 10.5 or 13.2 days. - These extreme values often stem from drivers with insufficient data. - **Improvement**: Apply a filter to include only active drivers (those with a sufficiently representative number of trips; for example, `num_rides >= 5` or `10`). ```Python rides4.where((rides4.mean_days_between_rides.isNotNull()) & (rides4.num_rides >= 5)) ```
**Formatting and rounding decimals (`round`)** - The `mean_days_between_rides` column displays an excessive number of irrelevant decimal places (e.g., 8.166666666666666, 7.428571428571429), making it difficult to read. - **Example**: ```Python from pyspark.sql.functions import round rides4 = rides4.withColumn("mean_days_between_rides", round("mean_days_between_rides", 2)) ```
**Using more robust statistical metrics (median or percentiles)** - The mean is sensitive to outliers—such as drivers who complete two trips on the same day, or those who take months between trips. - Calculating the median (50th percentile) or the standard deviation, in addition to the mean, will provide a better understanding of the data distribution (i.e., driver behavior).
**Filtering same-day trips or calculating in hours instead of days** - There are many records where `mean_days_between_rides = 0.0` (representing drivers who completed multiple trips on the same day). - Evaluate the time interval in hours rather than days if the data granularity requires analyzing multiple consecutive trips within a single day.
**Leverage the visualization capabilities of Apache Zeppelin (%display)** - Use Zeppelin’s native visualization integration—replacing `.show(10)` with the `%sql` command—to generate interactive bar charts, box plots, or histograms.

# Lab
---

paragraphs.title: 1 - What is the average time between rides for each driver?
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Define the window specification:
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
driver_ws = Window.partitionBy("driver_id").orderBy("date_time")

# Generate date and time of previous ride, number of days between current ride
# and previous ride, and mean days between rides for each driver:
from pyspark.sql.functions import count, datediff, lag, mean
driver_ride_days = rides \
  .withColumn("date_time_previous", lag("date_time").over(driver_ws)) \
  .withColumn("days_between_rides", datediff("date_time", "date_time_previous")) \
  .groupBy("driver_id") \
  .agg(count("*").alias("num_rides"), mean("days_between_rides").alias("mean_days_between_rides"))

# List busy and not-so-busy drivers:
driver_ride_days.orderBy("mean_days_between_rides").show(10)
driver_ride_days.orderBy("mean_days_between_rides", ascending=False).show(10)
